effect_mechanism: Trees kept in or added to farmland hold more species than the treeless or simplified land use they replace. Pooled over 47 publications, silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures; systems with native, unplanted trees were 36.3% above open pasture against 20.9% for planted systems, and invertebrate biodiversity in native-tree systems was 53.7% above open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]. For coffee and cacao, a global meta-analysis (De Beenhouwer et al. 2013) found total species richness fell by 46%, and forest-species richness by 65%, when traditional agroforest was compared with sparse-shade plantation, because the diverse, structurally complex shade canopy lets more species persist [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_2]. A meta-analysis of cocoa found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and a review reports bird diversity between 120 and 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems (Gordon et al. 2007) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. Across tropical agroforestry interventions, natural enemies of pests were significantly more abundant than in the same crop without trees [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1]. In a ten-year trial on degraded lateritic soil in West Bengal, India, earthworm diversity (Simpson's index) was 0.62 in a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system against 0.41 in sole pigeon pea [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. In Colombia, intensive silvopastoral systems are reported, citing earlier studies, to carry four times more birds and 35% higher bird species richness than grass monocultures and 62% higher ant species richness than treeless pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2]; a World Bank silvopastoral operation reported increased species richness and abundance, including many forest-dependent and endangered species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]; and silvopastoral projects significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Niger, FMNR adoption appears to increase tree diversity by between one and three tree species per farm [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1], and the Kenyan WOCAT compiler notes that FMNR sites provide more habitats than degraded sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity]. Farmers in Colombia and Costa Rica see live fences as corridors for fauna and flora [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6].

effect_mechanism: A review of nature-based solutions states that agroforestry is likely to have biodiversity benefits compared with conventional arable, pasture or forestry land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3]. A pan-tropical meta-analysis of agroforestry against the same crops grown without trees found natural enemies of pests significantly more abundant under agroforestry [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1].
conditionality: More enemies is not the same as more kinds of enemy: in the same meta-analysis the majority of studies (7 out of 11) showed no effect of agroforestry on enemy diversity, and the response of predation and parasitism was mixed, with 3 of the 7 studies showing no effect [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2]. The benefit therefore rests on abundance of a functional group, not on species richness. The review makes the benefit depend on the variety, abundance and ecological suitability of the tree species used, and its statement is a synthesis of a cited European meta-analysis carrying no effect size [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3]. Neither source states how large the gain is, so the strength is not quantified. The meta-analysis is almost entirely tropical (shaded coffee, cocoa and plantain, alley cropping and improved fallows, with maize the commonest crop), the closer match to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1].

effect_mechanism: On red and lateritic soils in Jhargram, West Bengal, India, an agri-horti-silviculture system of Gmelina arborea and grafted mango trees with pigeon pea grown in the alleys had the highest earthworm diversity of the systems compared, with a Simpson's diversity index of 0.62 against 0.41 in sole pigeon pea [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. Tree prunings and leaf fall were kept in the field.

effect_mechanism: Shade trees over coffee and cocoa hold species that sun plantations lose. A global meta-analysis of coffee and cacao by De Beenhouwer et al. found total species richness fell by 46%, and forest-species richness by 65%, when traditional agroforest under a diverse, mostly indigenous shade canopy was compared with plantation under sparse shade of one or a few tree species; the structurally complex canopy lets more species persist [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_2]. A meta-analysis of cocoa found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and a review reports, from Gordon et al. (2007), bird diversity between 120 and 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. In Nicaraguan coffee, most certification schemes had a tree-diversity index, used as a proxy for habitat quality, that rose against non-certified farms [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1].
conditionality: The gains are measured against sun or sparse-shade plantations. Against natural forest, agroforest held 11% fewer species in total and 35% fewer forest species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_4]; that marks a ceiling, since shade cropping replaces plantation or farmland rather than forest, not a loss caused by the practice. The other harm finding is a yield trade-off in Cameroonian cocoa: yields above 1 t/ha did not seem attainable with more than 10 associated species, while about 750 kg/ha was possible with up to 20-23 species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. Scheme design matters: C.A.F.E. Practices was the only Nicaraguan certification scheme under which tree diversity fell [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. The bird figure and the Nicaraguan result are second-hand readings, and the review notes the shaded coffee systems had an overall decline in yield [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. The coffee and cacao meta-analysis draws on Latin America, Asia and Africa, most of it Latin American [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1]; the cocoa meta-analysis draws mainly on lower-middle-income countries [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1]. The cocoa and coffee units from single crops enter under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling.

In the Colombian Amazon piedmont, silvopastoral projects significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties, which enters as a forest-cover component [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Colombia, intensive silvopastoral systems held four times more birds and 35% higher bird species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures in the same landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2].
conditionality: The comparator matters: the meta-analysis gain is against open pasture, and the same table reports negative log response ratios for silvopasture compared with native forest, so the benefit applies where trees are added to treeless pasture, not where silvopasture replaces forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. The envelope is adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target: the measured project outcome is from upper-middle-income Colombia and the meta-analysis carries no income-group tag, so transfer to low-income pastoral systems is not established by these units [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. effect_mechanism: Trees added to cropland and pasture store carbon in their biomass and soil, and the row's class rests on the evidence that sets that storage against the other greenhouse gases. A global synthesis combining carbon sequestration in biomass and soil with changes in net methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions estimated that a shift to agroforestry can mitigate 27.2 (± 13.5) t CO2 eq per hectare a year, at least over the early growth stage up to an average age of 14 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_1]. In Colombia, a preliminary balance by Naranjo et al. (2012), cited in a Spanish-language review, found that in intensive silvopastoral systems lower nitrogen losses and greater carbon capture offset the methane emitted by the cattle [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2]. The storage evidence itself is large and consistent in direction. A global meta-analysis found agroforestry systems stored an average of 46.1 Mg C/ha (95% confidence interval 36.4–55.8) in tree biomass and increased soil organic carbon stocks by an average of 25.9% (17.4–34.4%), with a greater gain where trees were established in cropland than in pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_ma20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_2]; another put soil carbon stocks under agroforestry at 126 Mg C·ha−1, 19% more than in cropland or pasture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_1]; and the global synthesis reports soil carbon sequestration between about 0.5 and 2 t C per hectare a year at sites less than 10 years old, with none of the compiled studies reporting carbon losses [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kim16_1]. IPCC assessments state that agroforestry accumulates between 0.59 and 6.24 t ha–1 yr–1 of carbon above-ground at field scale, with below-ground carbon often 25% or more of the gains, and describe large mitigation benefits from increasing carbon sinks in vegetation and soils [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6ch5_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccsrccl6_1]. Meta-analyses report more soil organic carbon under agroforestry than under controls or crop monocultures in sub-Saharan Africa (RR 1.2), the tropics (overall effect size 1.21) and West African fields with shrubs and trees (+ 20 to 75%) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1]; a global synthesis for IPCC Tier 1 coefficients found a mean stock change factor of 1.25 for croplands converted to agroforestry [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_1]. East African agroforestry systems stock an average of 24.2 Mg C ha−1 in biomass and 98.8 Mg C ha−1 in the soil [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muthuri23_1]. In shaded tree crops, total biomass carbon in cocoa agroforestry is on average 2.5 times higher than in a monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1], a coffee agroforestry farm in Costa Rica stored a mean 3.6 t C/ha/yr over eight years of eddy-covariance measurement [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5], and shaded coffee plots held 29,8 Mg ha-1 more above-ground biomass carbon than full-sun plantations [ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. In Costa Rican silvopasture, carbon storage potential was 1.2 to 4.5 Mg ha-1 yr-1 against less than 1 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in pastures without trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. In Ethiopia, regeneration projects at Humbo and Soddo report 181,650 and 94,817 tonnes of CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_12], and the Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler notes that increasing tree cover through FMNR is one of the ways to sequester carbon in biomass [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Avoided deforestation by silvopastoral projects in Colombia, compared with control properties, enters as a forest-cover component with no carbon quantity attached [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Lempira, Honduras, soil organic matter under the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system, monitored for four years in three places, increased from 2.4% to 4.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].

effect_mechanism: Trees added to cropland or pasture remove carbon from the air and store it in two places: in standing tree biomass and in the soil. On the biomass side, a global meta-analysis of tree-based agroforestry (windbreaks, alley cropping, hedgerows, shelterbelts, silvopasture) found the systems stored an average of 46.1 Mg C/ha (95% confidence interval 36.4–55.8) in tree biomass, against adjacent cropland or pasture with no trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_ma20_1]. On the soil side, the same meta-analysis found agroforestry raised soil organic carbon stocks by an average of 25.9% (17.4–34.4%), with the larger gain where trees were established in cropland [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]; a second meta-analysis found soil carbon stocks under agroforestry of 126 Mg C·ha−1, 19% more than in cropland or pasture, driven by litter from tree pruning and root inputs [ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_1]; and the IPCC Tier 1 revision put the soil carbon stock change factor for cropland converted to agroforestry at 1.25 [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_1].
conditionality: What the land was before decides whether soil carbon storage rises. Converting cropland adds soil carbon, but converting pasture did not change soil carbon stocks in one meta-analysis, because perennial grass already supplies large below-ground carbon inputs [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4]; silvopasture had the lowest increase or no change against nearby pasture in another [ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3]; and the soil carbon change rate for grassland converted to agroforestry was not significantly different from zero (0.23±0.25 t C ha−1 yr−1) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_3]. effect_mechanism: Trees on rainfed cropland add carbon to the soil, mainly under their canopies, through litter and root inputs on soils depleted by annual cropping. A meta-analysis of semi-arid West Africa found that shrubs and trees on agricultural fields raised soil total carbon by 20 to 75%, an effect ascribed to litter deposition and sediment trapping under the canopies of woody perennials [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2]. effect_mechanism: IPCC assessments state that agroforestry accumulates above-ground carbon at field scale, with below-ground carbon often 25% or more of the gains, and the SRCCL describes large mitigation benefits from increasing carbon sinks in vegetation and soils [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6ch5_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccsrccl6_1]. Meta-analyses in sub-Saharan Africa and the humid tropics report more soil organic carbon under agroforestry than under controls or crop monocultures, used here as the soil-carbon component, and East African agroforestry systems stock an average of 24.2 ± 2.8 Mg C ha−1 in biomass [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_1]. A global synthesis built for IPCC Tier 1 coefficients found a mean soil organic carbon stock change factor of 1.25 for croplands converted to agroforestry [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_1]. Global meta-analyses comparing agroforestry with adjacent cropland or pasture find carbon removals in both biomass and soil: tree biomass held an average of 46.1 Mg C/ha (95% confidence interval 36.4–55.8), soil organic carbon stocks rose by an average of 25.9%, with a greater gain where trees were established in cropland rather than pasture, and a separate synthesis found soil carbon stocks 19% higher, driven by litter from tree pruning and root inputs [ev_carbon_sequestration_ma20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_1]. effect_mechanism: Trees planted into cropland add carbon to the soil through leaf litter, prunings and roots, raising soil carbon storage above that of the crop grown alone. In a ten-year trial on degraded red and lateritic soil in West Bengal, India, soil organic carbon under a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea alley system reached 0.59% against 0.34% under sole pigeon pea, from an initial 0.30% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. A global meta-analysis found that converting cropland to agroforestry generally increased soil carbon storage, consistent with earlier syntheses [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]. In southern Malawi, Tephrosia vogelii relay-planted under maize keeps growing into the dry season and returns nitrogen-rich leafy residues; at Songani soil C under this intercrop was 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1].
conditionality: The direction is consistent, but not every site shows a clear gain. The Malawi difference was a trend that was not significant (P value = 0.10) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1], and at Sadore, Niger, the block with Ziziphus mauritiana trees held from 5 to 10 % more soil organic carbon than the block without after four years of millet and cowpea, a difference that was not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. The Niger trial compares two blocks with tree presence neither randomised nor replicated, so block differences are mixed into the contrast [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. Soil carbon is a component of carbon removal, measured here as a stock or concentration, not as a removal rate, and tree biomass storage is not counted in this row [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]. The strongest gain comes from a long-running research-station trial on degraded soil, where the starting carbon was low [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. The field evidence is from low-income Malawi and Niger and lower-middle-income India, all rainfed cropping; the meta-analysis is global [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3].

effect_mechanism: In Sudano-Sahelian cropland, shrubs and trees on agricultural fields had an overall positive but variable effect on soil total carbon (+ 20 to 75%), and a cited meta-analysis reports that soil under Faidherbia albida canopy holds on average 46 per cent more organic carbon than outside it [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. The externally audited Humbo FMNR project in Ethiopia reports CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that increasing tree cover through FMNR is one of the ways to sequester carbon in biomass [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. In Lempira, Honduras, soil organic matter under the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system, monitored for four years in three places, increased from 2.4% to 4.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].

effect_mechanism: Colombian project measurements attribute net CO2 removals to dispersed trees in pasture, live fences and intensive silvopasture, and a preliminary balance reports that greater carbon capture and lower nitrogen losses in intensive silvopastoral systems offset livestock methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2]. Spanish-language reviews add that silvopasture established from degraded woodland increases above- and below-ground carbon stocks and that tree-improved pastures and live fences scored as helping the mitigation pillar in a Colombian prioritisation [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. Avoided deforestation by silvopastoral projects in the Colombian Amazon piedmont, compared with control properties, also enters as a forest-cover component, with no carbon quantity attached [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg ha-1 yr-1, against less than 1 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in pastures without trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1].
conditionality: The Colombian figure is a project total with no per-hectare or per-year denominator, and the other units are cited secondary or expert-prioritisation statements without rates [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. The envelope is adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target: the evidence is from upper-middle-income Colombia, high-income Costa Rica and Latin America generally [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4]. The gain is mostly in tree biomass rather than soil: global meta-analyses find that converting pasture to agroforestry did not affect soil organic carbon stocks, and that silvopasture had the lowest increase or no change in soil carbon, because topsoil carbon under pasture already comes from perennial grass inputs [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3]. Carbon removals from silvopasture therefore depend on how many trees are added and kept, not on soil gains.

On the recharge side, the IPCC assessment states that agroforestry increases groundwater recharge in drylands when managed at moderate density (Ilstedt et al. 2016; Bargués-Tobella et al. 2020) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1], and, combining canopy interception and transpiration data of trees with their effects on water infiltration, Ilstedt et al. derived an optimal intermediate tree density for parklands from a groundwater-recharge perspective [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6]. On the water-use side, a review cites Wallace et al. effect_mechanism: Experimentally induced drought in an eastern Canadian soybean-intercropping agroforestry system caused crop losses in the monocrop only, while N-fixation declined in both systems [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. Households in Isiolo County, Kenya, describe trees that keep producing through drought: one farmer said they planted trees because "they do not dry up fast during times of drought", and another said of mango trees that their roots travel far and get water from deep down [ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7]. The same study's background, citing earlier reviews, names deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water and nutrients as one reason agroforestry species are resilient to droughts [ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. In its two communities 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind, respondents listed agroforestry as important for household livelihood during drought, and in Burat households practising agroforestry largely said droughts were less frequent (64 respondents) while most without it (46 respondents) said the opposite; the authors conclude that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought [ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10].

effect_mechanism: Two sources point to a slight reduction in drought damage. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].
conditionality: The cell is thin: one compiler judgement on a WOCAT technology sheet from lower-middle-income Kenya [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts] and one promoter-written practitioner account from Honduras. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. Neither unit puts a size on the benefit or measures drought losses with and without the practice in a controlled comparison; an independent measured study is what is missing.

effect_mechanism: In a cocoa plantation in Ghana's Ashanti region, shade trees competed with cocoa for soil water through the extreme 2015/16 El Niño drought. All cocoa plants under the recommended leguminous shade tree Albizia ferruginea died; cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria, the most common shade tree, suffered 77% mortality and massive stress, with sap flux density cut to 115 g cm2 day1 against 170 in full sun; and sap-flux recovery after the drought was 163 in full sun against 37 under Antiaris. Soil water content was higher in full sun than under the shade trees, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].
conditionality: This is a single measured study on a single farm with a few replicate shade trees per species, so the row gives a direction only, with no size class [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. The shade-tree species is part of the result: the loss was total under Albizia and heavy under Antiaris, so other shade species, densities or pruning regimes may behave differently. The drought was extreme; the same plots were also measured through wet and normal dry periods, which separates the drought response from ordinary shade effects [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. The finding is crop-specific (cocoa) and enters under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling; Ghana is lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target. A financed shade-cocoa system in a drought-prone area carries this as a risk to the planted asset and the crop.

effect_mechanism: Tree shade lowers temperatures where crops and animals sit: poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot days, Faidherbia albida canopies lowered midday air temperature over Ethiopian wheat by up to 6°C against the open field, and reviews report shade buffering temperature effects by 2–4°C and lowering ambient temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. Shade from live fences and silvopastoral models reduces cattle heat stress, and a Brazilian comparison found 20 to 100% reductions in areas at critical thermal-comfort levels for animals [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8, ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Associated trees buffer air and soil temperature, reduce wind and raise humidity under the canopy, and tree cover protects crops against extreme microclimate fluctuations [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9, ev_microclimate_buffering_taboada20_3, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. A systematic review of dairy silvopasture, mostly in Brazil, found the effect on biophysical variables mostly (57%) favourable: silvopasture gave lower air, black globe and soil surface temperature, black globe humidity index and radiant thermal load than treeless pasture, and cows there showed fewer drinking events, lower surface temperature and lower respiratory rate [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1]; an older cattle review cites Kelly et al. (1950) that trees are the most effective shade, combining protection from sunlight with cooling as moisture evaporates from the leaves [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found summer air temperature 4.01% lower and relative humidity 13.45% higher in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. In tropical silvopasture, temperatures under tree crowns can average 2-5°C lower than outside them throughout the year, and under canopy trees averaging 20 m tall in tropical agroforestry systems temperature is about 2°C lower than at a site without trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a pan-tropical meta-analysis found mean temperature lower and daily extremes buffered in cocoa agroforestry against full-sun monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1], a coffee review reports, second-hand, that shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4], and shade reduced maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C in Costa Rican coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4]. In a Ghanaian cocoa field, the role of shade trees in moderating microclimate was confirmed especially in the dry and extremely dry periods, when daily mean maximum air temperatures were significantly higher, reaching up to 44°C, in the comparison with full sun [ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3].

effect_mechanism: Shade trees over coffee and cocoa lower the temperature the crop experiences. A pan-tropical meta-analysis found that the shade-tree canopy reduces solar radiation, so mean temperature stays lower and daily maxima and minima are buffered in cocoa agroforestry against full-sun monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1], and a coffee review reports, citing Lin et al. 2008 and Meylan et al. 2017, that shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, mitigating heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4]; the same review cites shade trees improving microclimate stability in Central America (Perfecto and Armbrecht 2003) [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7]. In Costa Rican coffee, measured shade reduced maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4], and the same tropical synthesis states, citing Avelino et al. 2011, that associated trees buffer air and soil temperature and raise humidity under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9]. A CATIE volume reports, from earlier tropical studies, about 2°C cooling under canopy trees averaging 20 m tall compared with a site without trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]. The IPCC, citing Ovalle-Rivera et al. 2015 and Schroth et al. 2015, notes that shade trees can ameliorate the rising stand temperatures that will significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. In a Ghanaian cocoa field study, the role of shade trees in moderating microclimate was confirmed especially in the dry and extremely dry periods, when daily mean maximum air temperatures were significantly higher, reaching up to 44°C, in the comparison with full sun [ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3].
conditionality: Every unit points to cooling, but the evidence does not state how much that reduces crop or income losses, so the strength is not quantified and the class is slight. effect_mechanism: In the dry Colombian Caribbean, silvopastoral models most intensive in shrubs, trees and rotational pasture reduce heat stress in cattle, and a Brazilian study found agroforestry reduced the area at critical thermal-comfort levels for animals by 20 to 100% compared with monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. In tropical silvopasture, temperatures under tree crowns can average 2-5°C lower than outside them throughout the year, depending on the characteristics of the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. A systematic review of silvopasture and dairy cattle, mostly from Brazil, found the effect on the thermal environment was mostly (57%) favourable: silvopasture gave lower air temperature, black globe temperature, soil surface temperature and radiant thermal load than treeless pasture, and cows drank less often and had lower surface temperature and respiratory rate [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1]. An older review cites Kelly et al. (1950) that trees are the most effective shade for cattle, adding evaporative cooling from the leaves to protection from sunlight [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].
conditionality: The Colombian and Brazilian review results are cited secondary findings from upper-middle-income settings, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. All units report air temperature, thermal indices or animal comfort, components of heat-stress impact rather than measured losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. Not every index moves: in the same systematic review, results for the temperature humidity index, which uses only air temperature and humidity, were unclear, with most of the studies that used it finding no significant difference between silvopasture and treeless pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. The cattle-shade statement from Australia and the USA is an old citation without a tree system [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].

effect_mechanism: The production evidence splits by sub-practice. Regeneration-based farmland, planted silvoarable systems and the cross-family syntheses each lean to a strong gain on their own, while silvopastoral, boundary and shaded perennial (coffee and cocoa) systems record both gains and losses. Meta-analyses report higher crop yield under agroforestry than controls in sub-Saharan Africa and higher soil nitrogen stocks than crop monocultures in the humid tropics, with soil nitrogen used here as a component of the production gap [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. In the Sahel, millet yields are reported to double or triple under Faidherbia albida and yields were higher where intensive FMNR is practised, and tree shade in pastures is associated with gains in milk production and weight gain [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_14, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded 23-26% more grain than open-field wheat in the normal seasons of 2013 and 2014, and up to 85% more in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low; available N close to the crowns was 35-55% larger than under sole wheat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_1]. Lower yield variability under more diverse shade is cited as a sign of greater yield resistance to shocks in shaded systems, and Kenyan agroforestry-project farmers in Lower Nyando raised farm productivity against a control group [ev_crop_yield_morel24_4, ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Fertilizer trees raise maize output: in Malawi, adopters had a 35% higher value of food crop production and 32% higher maize productivity than their counterfactual, and a review notes fertilizer tree species are widely documented to substantially increase maize yields compared with maize grown without fertilizer in Zambia and across Africa [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_lasco14_1]. In maize–Gliricidia trials run for 12-13 consecutive years in Malawi and Zambia, the intercrop gave the most stable yield at Makoka and more stable yields than fertilized maize at Msekera, and the intercrop with 50% of the recommended N and P fertilizer matched the yield of fully fertilized monoculture maize [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_2]. Maize yields were more stable with Leucaena hedgerows than in monocrop, as also shown for alley cropping and fertilizer trees [ev_yield_stability_lasco14_1]. In Maradi, Niger, millet yields rose by 120 to 209 kg/ha where FMNR was older than 6 years, with smaller increases for younger FMNR, and FMNR is estimated to have raised yields by an average of 100 kg/ha over 5 million hectares [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3]. In Lempira, Honduras, an ICRAF working paper reports that the Quesungual system raised maize yields from 1.9 to 3.2 tonnes per hectare and bean yields from 0.8 to 2.0 tonnes per hectare [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_2]. In Lempira, Honduras, farmers are reporting maize yield increases of a minimum of 60% after moving from slash-and-burn to the Quesungual system, and fields under continuous maize for seven years on 35% slopes and poor soil average 2.9 t/ha, against a best of 1.6 t/ha on the same fields before [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected than cereals, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. In subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. In Colombian intensive silvopasture, milk production was 32.1% higher than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture raises stocking rates up to four times above extensive grazing and with them meat and milk output per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1]. In Colombia, a Leucaena-based silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows ha-1 while eliminating chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During El Niño events, milk production fell by 2.2% in silvopastoral systems against 4.9% in conventional systems [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture compared with full sun, and dry-season weight gains were 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss (OR = 0.69) and a cocoa meta-analysis found total system yields about ten times higher than in monocultures [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_2]. Planted legume trees in maize systems hold up in synthesis: a meta-analysis of studies from West, East and southern Africa put the maize yield response ratio at 1.27–1.43 after rotational improved fallows of non-coppicing woody legumes and 1.11–1.30 with relay intercrops, against unfertilised maize, and the yield increase was 1.6 t ha−1 with coppicing woody legumes [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_3]. In the forest zone of Cameroon, maize grain yield in Leucaena alley plots rose from the first to the third year while yield in the treeless control fell, and groundnut in the alleys also out-yielded the control [ev_crop_yield_tonye95_1, ev_crop_yield_tonye95_2]. At Sadore, Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised sole millet yields by 41 % in the unfertilised control and by 10 % with farmyard manure, raised crop income by 5 to 14 % without counting the fruit, and from 2 to 3 times once fruit sales were included [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1, ev_crop_yield_bado21_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_2]. In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii intercropped in smallholder coffee and returned as mulch raised coffee yields by 400 kg ha−1, a 23–36% increase over the farmer's mulch practice across the two seasons [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1]. Among sub-Saharan adoption studies, high-quality maize studies show a significant gain for adopters (Cohen's d = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.12 to 0.42) [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]; a pest-control meta-analysis notes that the studies testing whether agroforestry pest control translated into crop yield both found it did [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]; and a hedgerow meta-analysis found plant hedgerows raised soil total N (SMD = 1.33; 95% CI 0.98–1.68) [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1].
conditionality: The sub-practices disagree, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence rather than a strong gain. On the gain side, regeneration-based farmland (Faidherbia albida and Piliostigma reticulatum parklands, FMNR in Niger and Ghana, the Quesungual system) and the cross-family meta-analyses and assessments show higher yields or soil nitrogen [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_15, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. On the conflicting side, shaded perennial systems pair those system-level gains with main-crop losses: cocoa yields 25% lower than in monocultures, coffee and cocoa yield per hectare 26% lower than conventional systems, and coffee yields declining under >60% shade, while shade did not prevent the drought-induced cocoa yield decline in a Ghanaian experiment [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the separator there is whether the by-crops are counted and how dense the shade is, and the units are crop-specific to coffee, cocoa and coconut. Planted silvoarable systems now lean to a gain, but still record tree–crop competition losses next to the fertilizer-tree and Gliricidia gains; silvopasture pairs Latin American milk and stocking gains with a global review's losses under dispersed trees; and boundary planting pairs higher yields within sheltered farmland with losses at shelterbelt edges and in windbreak paddocks [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The separator, in the sources' own terms, is spacing, tree density, tree age and distance from the tree line: alley spacings under 10 TH were predicted to reduce yields, pasture yield fell as tree density rose and under the oldest trees, livestock yield fell with more trees and older trees, and yield losses were reported up to 10 m from hedges in the rainy season and in shelterbelt edge zones [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_16, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The evidence pulls both ways: tree–crop competition for water delayed Kenyan maize and could cause crop failure, intercropped wheat in China and soybean in Brazil yielded less than monocultures, groundnut and millet yields fell under Cordyla pinnata in Senegal, and excess shade can reduce pasture productivity [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11, ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. The pooled magnitude combines a crop-yield response ratio with a soil-nitrogen response ratio, and a systematic review's pooled crop-yield effect across agroforestry interventions had a confidence interval spanning zero [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1]. The Lower Nyando productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant, earlier work cited in a temperate alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years, and the yield-variability finding is a cited statement [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. Gains are not universal: Malawian non-adopters would have lost food crop value had they adopted fertilizer trees, at Msekera fertilized monoculture maize out-yielded the maize–Gliricidia intercrop, and some stability models there ranked unfertilized control maize as more stable than the intercrop [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_3]. The Malawi estimates come from an ICRAF working paper evaluating an ICRAF-promoted technology, and the Gliricidia trials compare against fertilized maize rather than farmer practice [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1]. Cereals often lose: in Maradi, FMNR did not significantly increase grain yields, the income gain being attributed to crop diversification instead, and under parkland trees cereal grain yield ranged from a loss of 0.54 t ha-1 under Balanites aegyptiaca to a gain of 0.24 t ha-1 under F. albida, with reductions attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water [ev_crop_yield_haglund11_1, ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. The Niger yield figures are earlier estimates cited in a grey-literature review, and the Honduran yields are before-and-after case-study figures for a slash-and-mulch system [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1]. Next to the trees the effect reverses: crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. In the West African Sahel, live fences and fodder banks reduced yields in the first year, which recovered in the second [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Tree density matters: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. The Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Costa Rican livestock units are high-income evidence [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. A global quantitative review against treeless controls found average losses for windbreaks, alleys and dispersed trees: windbreak paddocks −8.3%, alleys −17.63%, pasture under dispersed trees −20.8% and livestock there −18.6%, with gains only at wide spacings (+13% at 15 tree heights between alleys, +8.04% across a windbreak paddock 20 tree heights wide) [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. Of the newer primary studies, regeneration-based farmland again holds the stronger result: The Ethiopian drought-year gain stays separate from the normal-season gain; at the same site soil total N did not differ significantly under and outside the canopy at the end of the 2013 season despite the larger available N near the crowns, and the yield benefit of canopy cooling is modelled and appeared only with applied N [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_2, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. The Ontario windbreak gain is high-income boreal evidence from a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site, with plots irrigated from ditches, so it does not test the water competition near trees that drives the dry-year losses [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. In southern Malawi a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop, which produces leafy residues but no grain, gave the same quantity of maize grain as monoculture maize fertilised in the same way, so no yield gain [ev_crop_yield_snapp10_1]. The newer evidence repeats these splits. Across sub-Saharan adoption studies agroforestry is not associated with a statistically significant effect on yield overall (Cohen's d = 0.35, 95% CI: −0.07 to 0.78, p = 0.14), the gain appearing only in the high-quality maize subset, and the review notes many adoption studies have weak causal identification [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1, ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]. At Sadore the Ziziphus gain depended on the fertiliser: millet yield fell by 13 % under the trees with NPK, intercropped millet fell by 4 and 11 % with NPK alone and with NPK and manure, and cowpea fell by 15 % in the unfertilised control, probably from tree shade, though it rose 9% with NPK [ev_crop_yield_bado21_3, ev_crop_yield_bado21_7, ev_crop_yield_bado21_4, ev_crop_yield_bado21_5, ev_crop_yield_bado21_6]; soil N there did not differ significantly with and without the trees, and tree presence was neither randomised nor replicated across the two blocks [ev_soil_nitrogen_bado21_1]. Young fruit trees compete hard: between juvenile plumcot rows in irrigated semi-arid Xinjiang, China (upper-middle income), soybean yield fell by 46.03% and alfalfa by 51.83% against sole crops, partly because the intercrop had a smaller cropped area and lower seeding rate [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In the Rwandan coffee trial the Tephrosia gain was significant only in the first season [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_2], and a review of dairy silvopasture found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. The Sileshi maize meta-analysis compares against unfertilised maize, not farmer practice with fertiliser, and its authors note signs of publication bias [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1]; the hedgerow meta-analysis mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. The Honduran yield figures are farmer reports relayed by the project's promoters in a grey-literature article and a before-and-after comparison with the best earlier yield, not a concurrent control; the gain belongs to the bundle of trees, mulch, zero tillage and no burning, not to the trees alone [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6].

effect_mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings, studies disagree on whether agroforestry narrows the production gap: livestock and sheltered-crop systems mostly gain, while crops intercropped with trees often lose output. Gains: wheat and barley intercropped 2.5 m from trees in Iran out-yielded monocultures by 35% and 39% [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2]; a meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland, alongside microclimatic improvements [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]; tree leaves added about 40 kg ha-1 of nitrogen in a Brazilian cactus pear and buffel grass system [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]; and on the livestock side, Brazilian silvopasture gave higher daily bodyweight gain per animal, Colombian intensive silvopasture gave 32.1% more milk than the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, stocking reached 4.3 cows ha-1 while chemical fertiliser was eliminated, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Under drought, forage in a Colombian silvopastoral system stayed constant while grass monoculture biomass fell to 25%, deep-rooted trees give more stable dry-season forage, milk fell by 2.2% against 4.9% in conventional systems during El Niño events, and at El Hatico milk still rose 10% in 2009, the driest year in decades at 440 mm [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Losses: intercropped wheat in China and maize in Indonesia yielded significantly less than monocultures, and Brazilian soybean gave about 500 and 700 kg ha-1 against about 3000 and 2700 kg ha-1 in monoculture, attributed to lower radiation [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]; in a drip-irrigated trial in Xinjiang, China, soybean intercropped between juvenile plumcot rows yielded 46.03% less than sole-cropped soybean and intercropped alfalfa 51.83% less [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]; crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]; and dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. In perennial crops, shaded coffee in Paraná, Brazil yielded up to 101.99 kg/ha in its second year where the unshaded monoculture control yielded zero [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1], and a coconut review reports, second-hand, increased nut yields when pasture, black pepper and coffee were intercropped with coconut [ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1].
conditionality: Gains and losses both carry material weight, so no direction is stated; what separates them is visible in the evidence. Production system: the livestock and silvopasture units are almost all gains, while the losses are concentrated in crops intercropped with trees, where shading and competition reduce the crop [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3]; the Chinese plumcot losses were measured with the crop rows only about a metre from young trees [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1]. Distance and density: within one Chinese meta-analysis, yield rose across sheltered farmland but fell in the edge zone next to the trees, and the figures are not to be netted [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]; in Colombia, dense Acacia lowered milk per cow while sparser planting raised it [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. Management: the soybean loss is attributed to radiation, which the authors tie to pruning and management of the system [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]. For a Task Team Leader, the actionable distinctions are system type, tree spacing and density, and canopy management. On evidence quality, the plumcot intercrop is a direct randomised trial, while most other units on both sides are earlier results cited in Portuguese- or Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the shelterbelt meta-analysis is the main primary synthesis and supplies one figure on each side [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. The nitrogen unit is a soil-fertility component rather than a yield measure [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7], and the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year, with the Colombian forage result likely describing the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Some silvopasture evidence also finds no difference: a systematic review of dairy silvopasture, mostly in Brazil, reports that the studies that evaluated milk production did not find a significant difference from treeless pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. Under shocks the perennial-crop evidence finds no shade effect either way: cocoa yield loss in the Bahian drought was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover, and Mexican coffee farms lost 18 to 40% of their harvest after a hurricane regardless of vegetation management [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The Paraná coffee result depends on tree species and development, and the coffee and coconut units are crop-specific [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1].

effect_mechanism: In rangeland and pasture systems trees raise livestock output through forage, shade and higher stocking. In the Senegalese Ferlo, herbaceous biomass under Acacia tortilis and Balanites aegyptiaca canopies was 2 to 5 times that of treeless areas, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle and 80 per cent of small-ruminant diets late in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. In Latin American silvopasture, tree shade is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]; milk was 32.1% higher in intensive silvopasture than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Stocking rises up to four times above extensive grazing, reaching 4.3 cows ha-1 in a Colombian Leucaena system that eliminated chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1, ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Milk rose 29% on high tree-density pasture against low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture against full sun, with dry-season weight gains 2 to 5% higher [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Under drought, forage held constant in a Colombian silvopastoral system while grass-monoculture biomass fell to 25 %, deep-rooted trees give steadier dry-season forage, cattle are better fed in critical drought periods, milk fell by 2.2% against 4.9% in conventional systems during El Niño events, and at El Hatico milk still rose 10% in 2009, the driest year in decades (440 mm) [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2, ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4].
conditionality: The row carries a harm signal tied to tree density: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture (1110 trees/ha) gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field, while the low-density stand (407 trees/ha) gave 16.6 L [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. Not every comparison finds a milk gain: a systematic review of mostly Brazilian dairy silvopasture found that the studies which measured milk production did not find a significant difference from treeless pasture, even where trees altered the thermal environment [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. What separates that null from the gains, as far as the evidence says, is the system: the gains come mostly from intensive silvopasture with fodder shrubs such as Leucaena and Tithonia, where the trees add feed as well as shade, while the Brazilian studies compare shade from exotic trees against treeless pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. Apart from that review, every unit is an earlier study read second-hand through a FAO country assessment, Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume, and none is a pastoral-system experiment run by the citing authors [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3]. The Senegalese diet shares describe how much of the ration comes from trees, not a measured production change [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. Most of the Latin American evidence is intensive silvopasture with Leucaena shrubs in upper-middle-income Colombia, the Brazilian review is upper-middle income, and the Costa Rican units are high-income; milk gains attributed to heat relief also reflect extra foliage and fruit [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1]. effect_mechanism: Linear tree plantings have been found both to raise and to lower yields. Gains come from shelter: windbreaks are reported to raise wheat yields by 15 to 20% by protecting plants from winter desiccation, protected plots in the Senegal River valley showed a 23 per cent total yield increase in the off-season, crop yield was 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland in a Chinese shelterbelt meta-analysis, and live fences can improve soil fertility and crop yields provided tree roots are deeper than crop roots [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_7, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_moran18_11]. In subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. A meta-analysis of plant hedgerows found they raised soil total N (SMD = 1.33; 95% CI 0.98–1.68), counted here as a component of the production gap; hedgerow litter and the capture of nutrient-laden sediment from runoff supply it [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. Losses come from competition and shade: crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2], greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts were found in dry years [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3], excess shade can reduce pasture productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14], and in the West African Sahel live fences and fodder banks reduced yields in the first year [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Hedgerow intercropping in a sub-Saharan meta-analysis gave a response ratio of 0.9, an interval touching no effect [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]. A global quantitative review of paddocks with windbreaks found yield reduced by 8.3% on average against paddocks with no windbreaks, excluding the land occupied by the trees, with more decreases (n = 171) than increases (n = 83): crop yield −9.2% and crop biomass −9.3%, while pasture showed a small average increase of +3.1% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_3, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]. Its distance-response curves nonetheless predict a total yield change of +8.04% across a paddock 20 tree heights wide [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5].
conditionality: The evidence itself names most of what separates gains from losses. Distance from the trees: the same Chinese meta-analysis reports the field-scale gain and the edge-zone loss, which are not to be netted [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2], and in Senegal yields fell within 10 metres of the hedges in the rainy season while the protected plots as a whole gained [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. Root depth: the live-fence benefit is conditional on tree roots lying deeper than crop roots [ev_crop_yield_moran18_11]. Season and dryness: losses near shelterbelts are greater in dry years [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. Time: the Sahel live-fence penalty was in the first year and yields recovered in the second [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Shade level: the pasture loss is from excess shade [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. These point to actionable design choices: species with deep roots, spacing and shade control, and accepting a first-year dip. At Bambey windbreak hedges had a neutral effect on groundnut [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_14]. On evidence quality, the hedgerow estimate is close to no effect rather than a clear loss [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]; most other units are cited secondary results, the wheat figure has no stated location, and the dry-year shelterbelt finding is temperate evidence [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_7, ev_crop_yield_moran18_11, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. Paddock geometry: the same review gives a pooled paddock loss and a predicted gain across a paddock 20 tree heights wide, so the width of the sheltered paddock relative to tree height separates loss from gain in its own data, consistent with the distance effect above [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. Crop type: in that review crop yield and biomass fell while pasture rose slightly, although the difference between yield types was not significant [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target, and its windbreak group also takes in hedgerows and native forest blocks [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The Ontario windbreak gain is high-income boreal evidence from a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site, with plots irrigated from ditches, so it does not test the water competition near trees that drives the dry-year losses [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. The hedgerow soil-nitrogen pool mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows and measures soil concentration, not yield, so it shows a pathway to higher output rather than the output itself [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1].

effect_mechanism: Fertiliser trees raised food crop value in Malawi, alley cropping roughly doubled crop yield against controls in a sub-Saharan meta-analysis, and wheat yield rose by 6.8% under reduced heat load in Indian agri-silviculture [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_3, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_3, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. A systematic review reports yield gains for soil-fertility replenishment practices where soil fertility is severely depleted, and in Ethiopia land productivity improved where nitrogen-fixing trees were incorporated into the farming system [ev_t6_yield_soilfert_castle21_2, ev_crop_yield_ieg20_1]. Fertilizer trees raise maize output: in Malawi, adopters had a 35% higher value of food crop production and 32% higher maize productivity than their counterfactual, and a review notes fertilizer tree species are widely documented to substantially increase maize yields compared with maize grown without fertilizer in Zambia and across Africa [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_lasco14_1]. In maize–Gliricidia trials run for 12-13 consecutive years in Malawi and Zambia, the intercrop gave the most stable yield at Makoka and more stable yields than fertilized maize at Msekera, and the intercrop with 50% of the recommended N and P fertilizer matched the yield of fully fertilized monoculture maize [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_2]. Maize yields were more stable with Leucaena hedgerows than in monocrop, as also shown for alley cropping and fertilizer trees [ev_yield_stability_lasco14_1]. A meta-analysis of woody legumes in maize across West, East and southern Africa found yield increases over unfertilized maize of 1.6 t ha−1 with coppicing woody legumes, and response ratios of 1.27–1.43 after rotational improved fallows and 1.11–1.30 with relay intercrops [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_3, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_2]. In Cameroon's humid forest zone, maize grain yield in Leucaena alley plots increased from the first to the third year while yield in the treeless control plot decreased, and groundnut pod yield was also higher in the alleys [ev_crop_yield_tonye95_2, ev_crop_yield_tonye95_1]. In the Sahel of Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees in the cropped block increased millet yields by 41 % in the control without fertilizer and by 10 % with farmyard manure, and millet yields in the millet/cowpea intercrop by 8 and 11 % in the same treatments [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1, ev_crop_yield_bado21_2, ev_crop_yield_bado21_6]; crop incomes rose 5 to 14 % without counting the tree's fruit, and 2 to 3 times with it [ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_2]. Across 333 paddock years in a global quantitative review, alleys reduced yield by 17.63% on average and only 69 responses showed increases; paddocks with spacings between alleys under 10 tree heights were predicted to lose yield, with a reduction of more than 25% under 2.5 tree heights, while at 15 tree heights the predicted paddock yield increase was 13% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8].
conditionality: The class is strong, but the harm side is real and the row records measured losses in several sources, so it is a strong average over a mix of gains and losses, not a gain everywhere. What separates them, as far as the evidence says, is the comparison and the inputs. The large gains are measured against unfertilized maize on depleted African soils, with leguminous trees supplying nitrogen [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_3, ev_t6_yield_soilfert_castle21_2]; once mineral fertiliser is applied, the tree benefit can vanish or reverse. In the Niger trial millet yield fell by 13 % with the trees under NPK fertilizer, and millet in the intercrop fell by 4 and 11 % with NPK alone and with NPK plus manure [ev_crop_yield_bado21_3, ev_crop_yield_bado21_7], and at Msekera fertilized monoculture maize out-yielded the maize–Gliricidia intercrop [ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1]. Crop choice matters too: in the same Niger trial cowpea yield fell by 15 % with the trees in the unfertilized control, probably from their shade, though it rose 9% with NPK [ev_crop_yield_bado21_4, ev_crop_yield_bado21_5]. Tree age and spacing matter: between juvenile plumcot rows in irrigated Xinjiang, China, intercropped soybean yielded 46.03% less and alfalfa 51.83% less than sole crops [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]; in a global review, alleys reduced paddock yield by 17.63% on average, narrow spacings lose yield and the largest spacings gain [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8]. Other losses: a Mozambique PES tree-planting programme lowered crop value, water competition with Grevillea robusta delayed Kenyan maize, intercropped wheat, maize and soybean yielded less than monocultures in China, Indonesia and Brazil, and Malawian non-adopters would have lost food crop value had they adopted fertilizer trees [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_2, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_2]; some stability models at Msekera ranked unfertilized control maize as more stable than the intercrop [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_3]. Some results sit at no effect: improved fallows were not significant in a Kenyan production-function estimate, a Tephrosia relay intercrop in southern Malawi gave the same quantity of maize grain as monoculture maize fertilised in the same way, and in Niger the soil with Ziziphus held 10 to 15 % more nitrogen than the soil without, a difference that was not significant [ev_crop_yield_place05_6, ev_crop_yield_snapp10_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_bado21_1]. Study caveats: the Niger trial placed its trees in a single block and the tree-free comparison in a separate block, so tree presence was not randomised and its contrasts carry block effects [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1]; the Malawi estimates come from an ICRAF working paper evaluating an ICRAF-promoted technology, and the Gliricidia trials compare against fertilized maize rather than farmer practice [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1]. The magnitude range runs from a single-digit wheat gain to a more-than-900% crop biomass gain under water stress in a Sahelian shrub intercrop, so it does not describe a typical effect [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]. The global alley review gives no country or income-group breakdown, and its alley group includes pasture alleys and hedges [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6]; the Xinjiang losses come from an irrigated upper-middle-income system with trees in their first years [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1]. For a project, the fertiliser regime, the crop grown in the alleys and the tree spacing are the design questions.

effect_mechanism: Millet yields are reported to double or triple under Faidherbia albida in Senegal, a cited meta-analysis reports mean yield increases of 150 per cent for maize and 73 per cent for sorghum under its canopy, and millet and groundnut yields were higher in plots with intensive FMNR [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_14]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded 23-26% more grain than open-field wheat in the normal seasons of 2013 and 2014, and up to 85% more in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low; available N close to the crowns was 35-55% larger than under sole wheat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_1]. Shrubs on Sudano-Sahelian fields often raised millet and sorghum yields (−25 to + 120%), and soil nitrogen was higher beneath shrubs and Faidherbia albida canopies, used here as a component [ev_crop_yield_felix18_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_felix18_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_faosen24_2]. In Maradi, Niger, millet yields rose by 120 to 209 kg/ha where FMNR was older than 6 years, with smaller increases for younger FMNR, and FMNR is estimated to have raised yields by an average of 100 kg/ha over 5 million hectares [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3]. In Lempira, Honduras, an ICRAF working paper reports that the Quesungual system raised maize yields from 1.9 to 3.2 tonnes per hectare and bean yields from 0.8 to 2.0 tonnes per hectare [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_2]. In Lempira, Honduras, farmers are reporting maize yield increases of a minimum of 60% after moving from slash-and-burn to the Quesungual system, and fields under continuous maize for seven years on 35% slopes and poor soil average 2.9 t/ha, against a best of 1.6 t/ha on the same fields before [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected than cereals, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1].
conditionality: Groundnut under Faidherbia albida behaved variably and groundnut and millet yields fell under Cordyla pinnata, so the effect depends on which trees are retained [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_10, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11]. The pooled magnitude draws on two soil-nitrogen percentages and an Ethiopian drought-season wheat gain reported as "up to" 85% [ev_soil_nitrogen_faosen24_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_felix18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2], and the Ghana figure is a share of households reporting higher yield [ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1]. Cereals often lose: in Maradi, FMNR did not significantly increase grain yields, the income gain being attributed to crop diversification instead, and under parkland trees cereal grain yield ranged from a loss of 0.54 t ha-1 under Balanites aegyptiaca to a gain of 0.24 t ha-1 under F. albida, with reductions attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water [ev_crop_yield_haglund11_1, ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. The Niger yield figures are earlier estimates cited in a grey-literature review, and the Honduran yields are before-and-after case-study figures for a slash-and-mulch system [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1]. The Ethiopian drought-year gain stays separate from the normal-season gain; at the same site soil total N did not differ significantly under and outside the canopy at the end of the 2013 season despite the larger available N near the crowns, and the yield benefit of canopy cooling is modelled and appeared only with applied N [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_2, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4].
