effect_mechanism: Shade trees over coffee and cocoa have been found both to raise and to lower production. Gains: a coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss (OR = 0.69) and improved continuous outcomes such as yield and bean quality (SMD = +0.42) against conventional systems [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_2]; a cocoa meta-analysis found total system yields about ten times higher than in monocultures, and a Bolivian cocoa study cited second-hand found total production three times higher [ev_crop_yield_niether20_2, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_9]; in Ethiopian smallholder coffee, leguminous shade and canopy openness benefited yields, including in the El Niño shock years [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_3]; and second-hand reports cite moderate shade yielding up to 3% more than full-sun coffee, reduced biennial yield oscillation, lower yield variability under diverse shade, intercropped coconut yielding more nuts, nitrogen fixation around 100 kg ha-1 by Erythrina or Inga shade, and in Paraná shaded coffee yielding up to 101.99 kg/ha where the unshaded control yielded zero [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4, ev_yield_stability_montagnini15_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_villa20_12, ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]. In southern Rwanda, sowing the legume shrub Tephrosia vogelii in the alleys of smallholder coffee and applying it as mulch raised coffee yield by 23–36% over the trial, a further 25–42% when NPK fertilizer was added, though the gain was statistically significant only in the first season [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1, ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_2]. Losses: main-crop yield per hectare was 26% lower in shaded coffee and cocoa than conventional systems and cocoa yields 25% lower than in monocultures [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_1]; second-hand reports cite cocoa productivity 41% higher in monocultures, a 30% coffee yield reduction once shade was established, 41% fewer coffee fruits under 40 to 60% Erythrina shade, significant productivity reductions under Organic-certified shade coffee, and a cocoa yield ceiling at high carbon storage [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_4, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6].
conditionality: What separates the sides, in the sources' own terms, is first what is counted and second how much shade. The gains in total system output count the by-crops and timber, while the losses are in the main crop alone: the same cocoa meta-analysis reports cocoa yields 25% lower but total system yields about ten times higher [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_2]. Shade density: coffee yields declined under >60% shade with 30 to 60% shade most favourable, fruit set fell under 40 to 60% Erythrina cover, and shaded systems under 30 % cover did not differ from full sun, management intensity driving yield instead [ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3]. Drought does not reliably favour shade: in the Ghanaian experiment shade did not prevent the drought-induced cocoa yield decline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2], cited work reports tree–cacao water competition pushing yields below open-sun levels [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8], Bahian cocoa drought losses were unrelated to shade-tree cover and Mexican hurricane harvest losses unrelated to shade management [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6], and diverse shade showed no direct benefit in the El Niño shock [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. Several units find no difference: in a Costa Rican case study no yield loss from shade was recorded, coconut yields are not strongly affected by interspace trees except where they block light, galangal yield was unaffected by over-canopy, soil nitrogen did not differ in cocoa systems, and young shaded coffee did not differ in fruiting nodes [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_2, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_2, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_3, ev_soil_nitrogen_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_villa20_2]; the coffee meta-regression found no moderator, shade density included, that significantly explained the variance [ev_crop_yield_patil25_9]. The evidence is crop-specific to coffee, cocoa and coconut; the Rwandan Tephrosia gain comes from a mulch-producing legume intercrop rather than from shade trees [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1]; the Ghanaian shade came from nets rather than trees, and the certification loss bundles shade with Organic certification rather than isolating it [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_4]. Many units are earlier studies read second-hand through Portuguese-, Spanish- or French-language reviews [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6].

effect_mechanism: Trees in pasture have been found both to raise and to lower production. Gains, mostly from Latin American intensive silvopasture and shaded pastures: Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain, Brazilian silvopasture gave a higher mean bodyweight gain per animal (512 g day-1) than monoculture (452 g day-1), and tree leaves added about 40 kg ha-1 of nitrogen in a Brazilian semi-arid system [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. In Colombian intensive silvopasture, milk production was 32.1% higher than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture raises stocking rates up to four times above extensive grazing and with them meat and milk output per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1]. In Colombia, a Leucaena-based silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows ha-1 while eliminating chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During El Niño events, milk production fell by 2.2% in silvopastoral systems against 4.9% in conventional systems [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture compared with full sun, and dry-season weight gains were 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Losses come from a global quantitative review of dispersed trees in pasture: pasture yield fell by 20.8% on average against control plots, by a predicted 30% where tree density exceeded 800 trees per hectare, and to below 50% of the control under the oldest trees, while livestock yield fell by 18.6% on average, declining with more trees up to ~300 trees per hectare and with increasing tree age [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_16].
conditionality: The Brazilian and humid-tropic units are cited secondary results, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target; the nitrogen unit is a component rather than a productivity measure [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. Tree density matters: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. The Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Costa Rican units are high-income evidence, and the milk gains attributed to heat relief also reflect extra foliage and fruit [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1]. What separates the sides: tree density and tree age, since in the review newly planted trees had no impact on pasture yield while dense and old stands cut it, and the dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture above also gave less milk than the open field [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_11, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12]; and the system, since the gains are intensive silvopasture with Leucaena shrubs or shaded pasture assessed on milk and weight gain, while the review pools paddock trees and silvopasture against treeless controls. Measured dairy evidence is thinner than the cited gains suggest: a systematic review of silvopasture for dairy cows, mostly from Brazil, found no significant difference in milk production between silvopastoral systems and treeless pasture in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. Even in the review a third of livestock paddock years (33%) gained [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target.

effect_mechanism: Household income and economic return are used as proxies for rural poverty [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. Across sub-Saharan Africa, a systematic review and meta-analysis found that agroforestry adoption raises income (Cohen's d = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.44, p < 0.001) [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]. Gains include Senegalese FMNR households earning more from non-timber products than non-adopters, calliandra fodder raising dairy farmers' net income in Kenya and Uganda, and a windbreak hedge in Senegalese irrigated rice with an internal rate of return of 36 per cent [ev_household_income_seghieri19_12, ev_household_income_kiptot11_1, ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet records higher farm income, its compiler crediting additional sources of income from the sale of wood, honey, medicinal components and non-wood products [ev_household_income_wocat_507_2019_farm_income]. Across World Vision FMNR projects, participant households were nine percentage points more likely than non-participants to report a decrease in poverty in their communities, reported similarly by poorer and female-headed households [ev_rural_poverty_wvfmnr19_10]. In Rwanda, food-insecure farmers more often sold tree products for income than food-secure farmers, and in Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought and in Lower Nyando held more livestock wealth than control households [ev_household_income_ndoli21_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_2]. In Maradi, Niger, FMNR adoption increased gross annual household income by between 46 and 56 USD per capita compared with propensity-matched non-adopters, and the annual benefit-cost ratio of practising FMNR was estimated at between 2.5 and 3.0 [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_economic_return_haglund11_1]. In south-central Niger, sales of fuelwood and service wood from FMNR raise the income of all social categories, even the vulnerable and very vulnerable, and the net present value of FMNR at 10% over 20 years was €772 per hectare [ev_household_income_abasse23_1, ev_economic_return_abasse23_1]. Fertilizer trees limit financial risk in drought years: where a crop fails, farmers using inorganic fertilizer lose the US$164 spent on the input, against US$90 for farmers who planted fertilizer trees [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1]. In a Mozambique carbon-forestry scheme promoting almost exclusively agroforestry, overall household income was generally increased [ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. In Colombia, intensive silvopasture had an operating benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 against 1.34 for a traditional system, and producer income from milk sales was 42.12% higher than under pasture monoculture owing to a higher carrying capacity [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1, ev_household_income_montagnini15_1]. In the Nepal mid-hills, after a market-oriented agroforestry project of fodder-tree hedgerows and understorey cash crops, bundled with marketing support, training, seed subsidies and organic fertiliser, the share of participating households below the poverty line dropped from 48 % to 34 % and the average farm-income figure rose from 37 to 48 percent, mainly from understorey crops, while off-farm income changed by -9% [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. In southern Malawi, under higher fertiliser prices the value-cost ratio of a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop with maize stayed above 4.0, which the authors call a profitable scenario, while the higher prices pulled monoculture maize down to 2.5 or less [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a meta-analysis found the average net return of shaded systems significantly higher by 23% than conventional systems [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_1], a case cited second-hand found a coffee price crash cut sun-coffee net revenue far more than that of extensive agroforestry [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_3], and a farm model for Costa Rica and Guatemala found smaller losses for high-shade systems under a 50% coffee price fall [ev_economic_return_lalani24_2]. Field trials of trees with crops add returns from several systems. In south-western Nigeria, net present values of a young sweet orange orchard were N -37900 monocropped against N 154300 intercropped with chilli pepper and amaranthus, N 105900 with cassava and maize and N -300 with egusi melon then soyabeans, because the intercropped plots yielded revenue throughout while the monocrop earned nothing in the first two years [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_2, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_3, ev_household_income_aiyel01_4]. In Sudan, crops grown in an Acacia senegal plantation earned more net revenue per hectare than sole crops: 558 against 501 SDG for sorghum, 300 against 205 for sesame and 518 against 389 for roselle [ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_fadl13_5, ev_economic_return_fadl13_6]. In Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping without fertiliser gave net benefits of 4148 against 2386 US$ per hectare for the traditional treeless system, the only alternative not dominated in the trial [ev_economic_return_tonye95_1]. On degraded lateritic soil in West Bengal, India, net returns of a Gmelina–mango–pigeon pea system were 2.66 times those of sole pigeon pea over a decade, with a surge in the final year from the Gmelina timber harvest [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1]; in Haryana, India, eucalyptus boundary strips gave a benefit–cost ratio of 3.5: 1 over the first rotation (Ram et al. 2011, reported in a review) [ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3]. In Rwandan smallholder coffee, Tephrosia mulch grown within the coffee gave the largest gross margins and returns to labour and the most favourable benefit–cost ratio (5.5) [ev_economic_return_bucagu13_4]. In Nigeria, maize mulched with tree prunings returned higher net benefits than nitrogen fertilizer or no input when the land for the trees was not valued [ev_economic_return_korm99_5]; in Xinjiang, China, plumcot intercrops had a higher average cash flow than the corresponding sole crops in the establishment years [ev_economic_return_wang23_1]; in West Java, Indonesia, a study by Rahman et al. (2017), cited in a systematic review, found agroforestry systems compared well with swidden cultivation on net present value and benefit-cost ratio [ev_economic_return_ntawu23_2]; and in the East Usambara Mountains of Tanzania, cash-crop revenues and total income were significantly higher under improved agroforestry than under traditional methods [ev_household_income_reyes05_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, from the first year onwards Quesungual farmers can rent their plots for livestock grazing because the system produces more stover [ev_household_income_welc02_7].
conditionality: Results are mixed: one systematic review's pooled income effect is small and not statistically significant, though the more recent sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds a significant one [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]; crop–fruit tree intercropping in China lowered gross household income, silvopasture income lags traditional pasture in the first years, and Regreening Africa found average tree-product income unchanged [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_household_income_castle21s_2, ev_economic_return_diasf08_1, ev_household_income_rgaf23_6]. Several gains are self-evaluations, bundled-project results or a modelled business case, and the proxies measure income or returns rather than poverty itself [ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5, ev_household_income_cmscr20_6]. The WOCAT farm-income unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not a household survey result [ev_household_income_wocat_507_2019_farm_income]. The Colombian sustainable-ranching completion report found no measured poverty reduction at closing, because many silvopastoral systems were still in their establishment phase and project effects could not be separated from drought and other climatic events [ev_rural_poverty_cmscr20_9]. The World Vision poverty result is a self-reported community perception from participants [ev_rural_poverty_wvfmnr19_10]. The Lower Nyando livestock-wealth difference, used by the authors as an income surrogate, was not significant at conventional levels, and the timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_household_income_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Maradi income and benefit-cost figures come from a matched survey comparison, while the fuelwood and net-present-value figures are cited in a grey-literature review [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_household_income_abasse23_1, ev_economic_return_abasse23_1]. The Zambian loss comparison and Mozambique result are earlier findings cited in a working paper and a review [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1, ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. The Colombian ratio and milk-income figures are earlier studies cited in a Spanish-language systematic review and a CATIE edited volume [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1, ev_household_income_montagnini15_1]. The Nepal results come from a bundled project and are not credited in full to the trees: they are a before-and-after recall survey of participating households with no control group, and the share of the bundle due to agroforestry is not stated [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. The Malawian value-cost ratio is a fertiliser-price scenario on on-farm trial data, not measured household income [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. The shaded coffee and cocoa evidence also pulls both ways: in Guayas, Ecuador, technified cacao monoculture earned a higher net margin per hectare than organic or traditional cacao agroforestry [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1, ev_economic_return_perezneira16_2], a pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found higher total system production not reflected in higher revenues or net present values [ev_economic_return_niether20_1, ev_household_income_niether20_1], and after Hurricane Stan coffee management had no effect on economic losses in Mexico [ev_economic_return_philpott08_1]; these units are crop-specific, and the price-fall result is modelled [ev_economic_return_lalani24_2]. The new trial evidence shows what separates gains from losses. Land and labour: cut-and-carry tree mulch for maize is only profitable in land- and labour-abundant areas, and where land is scarce it is unprofitable in the short and long term, with marginal returns below zero [ev_economic_return_korm99_6]. Input costs: in West Bengal the benefit-cost ratio was higher for sole pigeon pea than for pigeon pea intercropped with Gmelina or mango, even though the full tree system earned more in total [ev_economic_return_biswas22_2, ev_economic_return_biswas22_1]. Time: the orchard and plumcot results are establishment-period returns, in which the crops pay while the trees are young [ev_household_income_aiyel01_4, ev_economic_return_wang23_1], and the Indian net return depends on a timber harvest in the final year [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1]. The Tanzanian comparison bundles trees with cash crops and cattle, and its improved farms also carried higher household overhead costs and hired more labour, so the income gain is not the trees' alone [ev_household_income_reyes05_1]. The sub-Saharan meta-analysis rests mostly on adopter-versus-non-adopter contrasts in Ethiopia, Kenya and Malawi [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]. The trial budgets (Nigeria, Sudan, Cameroon, India, China) are researcher-run plots priced at local markets, not household poverty measures, and the Xinjiang result is from an irrigated upper-middle-income system [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1, ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_tonye95_1, ev_economic_return_wang23_1]. The Honduran grazing-rent point is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no income figure, for a system bundled with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_household_income_welc02_7].

effect_mechanism: An East African systematic review counts income among the main livelihood benefits of agroforestry, diversifying rural livelihoods and acting as a safety net in climate shocks, and calliandra fodder raised dairy farmers' net income in Kenya and Uganda [ev_household_income_muthuri23_1, ev_household_income_kiptot11_1]. Brazilian agroforestry viability studies report favourable financial indicators, and diversifying production and income is said to reduce farmers' vulnerability to commodity price volatility [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_1, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_7, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_8, ev_household_income_seghieri19_8]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of sub-Saharan adoption studies, mostly from Ethiopia, Kenya and Malawi, found agroforestry adoption raises household income (Cohen's d = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.44, p < 0.001), from diversified revenue in fruit, timber and fuelwood [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]. In the East Usambara Mountains, Tanzania, cash-crop revenues, especially from cardamom, and total income were significantly higher on farms using improved agroforestry, and gross income per capita was US$ 157 against US$ 74 on traditional farms [ev_household_income_reyes05_1]. In Rwanda, tree products are a safety net: food-insecure farmers more often sold tree products for income than food-secure farmers [ev_household_income_ndoli21_1]. In Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought, and in Lower Nyando held more livestock wealth than control households [ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_2]. In a Mozambique carbon-forestry scheme promoting almost exclusively agroforestry, overall household income was generally increased [ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. In the Nepal mid-hills, after a market-oriented agroforestry project of fodder-tree hedgerows and understorey cash crops, bundled with marketing support, training, seed subsidies and organic fertiliser, the share of participating households below the poverty line dropped from 48 % to 34 % and the average farm-income figure rose from 37 to 48 percent, mainly from understorey crops, while off-farm income changed by -9% [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. In West Java, Indonesia, agroforestry had a higher net present value and benefit-cost ratio than swidden cultivation, according to a review's reading of Rahman et al. (2017) [ev_economic_return_ntawu23_2].
conditionality: Several units show no effect or a loss: the pooled systematic-review income effect is not statistically significant, Regreening Africa found average tree-product income unchanged and no short-term income change detectable, and some Brazilian system components were loss-making [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_household_income_rgaf23_6, ev_household_income_crs23_5, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6]. The Nepal results come from a bundled project and are not credited in full to the trees: they are a before-and-after recall survey of participating households with no control group, and the share of the bundle due to agroforestry is not stated [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. Across World Vision FMNR projects, participant households were nine percentage points more likely than non-participants to report a decrease in poverty in their communities, reported similarly by poorer and female-headed households [ev_rural_poverty_wvfmnr19_10]. In Maradi, Niger, FMNR adoption increased gross annual household income by between 46 and 56 USD per capita compared with propensity-matched non-adopters, and the annual benefit-cost ratio of practising FMNR was estimated at between 2.5 and 3.0 [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_economic_return_haglund11_1]. In south-central Niger, sales of fuelwood and service wood from FMNR raise the income of all social categories, even the vulnerable and very vulnerable, and the net present value of FMNR at 10% over 20 years was €772 per hectare [ev_household_income_abasse23_1, ev_economic_return_abasse23_1]. effect_mechanism: Returns to farmers, used here as a proxy for rural poverty, tend to be higher in shaded coffee and cocoa. A meta-analysis found the average net return of shaded systems significantly higher by 23% than conventional systems, with a trend toward a higher benefit-cost ratio (1.66 against 1.44) [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_1, ev_economic_return_jezeer17_2]. effect_mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry five and ten times better than controls for runoff and soil loss respectively [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis found agroforestry trees reduced soil erosion by 50% against crop monocultures, and stated mechanisms include greater soil cover and structure protecting against raindrop impact, roots aiding infiltration and reducing surface runoff, and live fences lowering runoff velocity; runoff reduction is used as a component [ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2, ev_runoff_reduction_watts22_2, ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_5]. A review compiling published field studies of agroforestry against its controls found average soil-loss reductions of 68% for silvopastoral systems, 66% for silvoarable agroforestry and 55% for linear tree plantings, with no significant difference among the system types, and average water-loss reductions of 73% for silvopastoral and 43% for silvoarable systems [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_2]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that, due to less wind and water erosion, the siltation of ponds and water pans is reduced [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. During Hurricane Mitch in October 1998, Honduran farmers practising the Quesungual system suffered less landslide damage than those using traditional slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. In Costa Rica and Nicaragua, runoff equalled 28-48% of rainfall on pastures without trees against less than 10% in silvopastoral systems [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1]. Runoff was higher on grass pasture than in tree-dominated fodder banks, so tree cover attenuates runoff and the soil erosion it causes [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. Within single sub-practices, live fences of Gliricidia sepium are used to prevent erosion, shade trees attenuate runoff and erosion by close to a factor of two against full-sun plots, and in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion erosion under silvopasture was 35.3 percent lower than on degraded pasture soils [ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_2, ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1]. In shaded perennial systems, a study on a Costa Rican coffee farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], and after Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report that soil erosion has been nearly stopped, and estimate nutrient loss through erosion at more than 10 times lower than under slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4].
conditionality: The strong class rests on the cross-practice syntheses, which agree on large reductions: the sub-Saharan and pantropical meta-analyses and the review of compiled field studies, whose averages hold across silvopastoral, silvoarable and linear plantings alike [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. Single-practice field evidence is often weaker than those averages, so the size a project can expect depends on site and practice [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The compiled-review percentages are simple averages of study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and they mix temperate and tropical studies [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1]. The shade-tree effect represents little at catchment scale on the andisols studied [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]. Site matters within a practice: erosion fell 35.3 percent in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion but only 5.4 percent in the Cesar River Valley [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The sub-Saharan authors warn the very large effect sizes could reflect publication bias and expect more modest effects with more studies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. Regreening Africa observed no large overall change in erosion prevalence and found no link between more trees on farm and lower erosion, the FMNR result is participants' reported erosion, and the Nicaraguan hurricane result bundles trees with terraces and contour planting [ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_3, ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_5, ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_9]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not an erosion measurement, and the siltation rating enters as a component [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. The Lower Nyando erosion finding is farmer-reported, not measured [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. The landslide and runoff results are earlier studies cited in a working paper, a CATIE edited volume and a Spanish-language review; the runoff units enter as components of erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1, ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1, ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. The Chiapas landslide results are crop-specific coffee evidence from a single hurricane, with the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends only marginal (P = 0.062) and no effect of nearby forest cover [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The Honduran erosion claim is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no measured erosion rate, and the effect belongs to the whole bundle of trees, mulch cover, zero tillage and no burning [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4].

effect_mechanism: The measured soil-water evidence points both ways, and timing and soil depth separate the two sides. On the side of more soil water, a sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds that agroforestry improved infiltration and soil moisture content compared to the control (RR 1.6 for soil moisture, with 70% of soil-moisture observations above RR 1) [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1], and in a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation under greater ground cover [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and in the second season's May water content in that system was much greater than in all other treatments at depths below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. Water use efficiency was also higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.97 against 0.15 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1998/99 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. At Sadore, Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised the rainwater use efficiency of sole millet by 17 and 47 % with farmyard manure and in the unfertilised control, and that of a millet/cowpea intercrop by 17 % in the control and 11 % with manure or phosphate [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. On the side of less soil water, under Faidherbia albida parkland in Ethiopia soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; in cocoa, a pan-tropical meta-analysis found soils under agroforestry significantly lower in volumetric water content than under full-sun monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1], and in a Ghanaian cocoa plantation the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa raised water uptake and reduced soil water below that under full sun [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]; at Makoka the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests that the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. Trees therefore draw down dry-season and subsoil water, while recharge-season soil water and whole-system water productivity favour them. Several measurements found no difference: topsoil moisture did not vary under Faidherbia [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2], and at Makoka the distribution of water in the profile was generally comparable in all cropping systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1], with no significant treatment effects in the second season, in the second season's October, or in December and January of the third season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]; the authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with associated crops [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet adds increased water availability, its compiler crediting an increase in water retention which increases the ground water levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. Rainfall over agricultural land can also shift with continental land cover, increasing with more upwind tree cover [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report 23% soil humidity in the driest month (April) against 8% in a traditional slash-and-burn field, a difference equivalent to 20mm of rainfall, or 20 more days that crops can be sustained without rain; they explain it by better infiltration through the soil cover and more soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1].

These units therefore count here, for water stress, and are held out of the production gap because they say nothing about crop yield. The upwind-rainfall shift is a continental-scale effect, not a field-scale one [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4]. Infiltration and groundwater-recharge findings for catchments are carried in the agroforestry catchment water yield rows.
